name: Wig (lace front)

lead: A lace front wig has a thin, skin-toned mesh at the front with hairs tied in by hand, so the hairline appears to grow from the skin. The payoff is an instant full head of hair, used for fashion and to conceal hair loss, including medical hair loss.

The lace blends with the skin at the hairline, and the hair is attached by pins, elastic or skin-safe adhesive. It works while worn and is removable; no trial has tested lace fronts specifically. In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities, lace fronts are discussed mainly as a way to conceal hairline loss.

paras: People choose full-lace or partial-lace versions in French or Swiss lace, trim the lace to the hairline, and secure it with pins, elastic or adhesive. They maintain it like hair with regular care and replace it as it wears.
Adhesives and tight attachment can irritate the scalp. Cost and replacement needs vary with materials. Wigs are not regulated as drugs.

chain: Hair covers thin or bald areas
angle.text: A lace front wig gives a full head of hair with a hairline that appears to grow from the skin, visible the moment it is worn. It is removable and used to conceal hairline loss.

lead: A lace front wig is a wig whose front hairline is made from a fine, skin-coloured mesh, usually called hair lace, into which individual hairs are tied by hand so that the hairline appears to grow from the skin.[1] The base is commonly made of French or Swiss lace, and full-lace and partial-lace versions also exist.[1]

Wigs in general are worn for fashion, theatre, protection of natural hair and convenience, and by people with medical hair loss, most often those undergoing chemotherapy or living with alopecia areata.[1] In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities, lace fronts are discussed mainly as a concealment option for hairline loss.

No clinical trial specific to lace front wigs is available. The cosmetic effect is immediate and removable, and the main documented considerations are cost, upkeep, and the effects of attachment methods on the scalp.
infobox: Hair prosthesis (wig) with hand-tied lace hairline
Human hair, animal hair or synthetic fibre on a lace foundation
Temporary; cosmetic only, removed at will

paras: Wigs are built from human hair, animal hair such as horse, goat or yak, or synthetic fibre.[1] Human hair of the best grade is unbleached, uncoloured and kept with its cuticles aligned, often marketed as Remy hair; synthetic fibre has no grain direction and is made in fixed colours.[1] Construction uses either silk-thread wefts sewn to a net foundation or individual strands hand-knotted onto a foundation.[1]

In a lace front, each strand of the front edge is knotted into a lace panel so the hairline resembles natural growth.[1] Pins or adhesives may secure the lace edges, and skin-safe adhesives are sometimes used to attach wigs to bald skin.[1]

Wigs have a long history. A statue of Princess Nofret wearing a wig dates to roughly 2613 to 2494 BC, and European men wore wigs as standard dress in the 17th and 18th centuries.[1] Synthetic modacrylic wigs from the 1960s made wigs more affordable.[1] Lace-front construction is described as increasingly popular among wearers.[1]

No dedicated study of lace front wig safety has been found. Related literature on hair systems attached to the scalp describes traction or pressure-related hair loss in some wearers; see the article on hair systems. Historically, wigs could harbour lice.[1]
